fetched_contents.text: Candida albicans—The Virulence Factors and Clinical Manifestations of Infection Abstract Candida albicans is a common commensal fungus that colonizes the oropharyngeal cavity, gastrointestinal and vaginal tract, and healthy individuals’ skin. In 50% of the population, C. albicans is part of the normal flora of the microbiota. The various clinical manifestations of Candida species range from localized, superficial mucocutaneous disorders to invasive diseases that involve multiple organ systems and are life-threatening. From systemic and local to hereditary and environmental, diverse factors lead to disturbances in Candida’s normal homeostasis, resulting in a transition from normal flora to pathogenic and opportunistic infections. The transition in the pathophysiology of the onset and progression of infection is also influenced by Candida’s virulence traits that lead to the development of candidiasis. Oral candidiasis has a wide range of clinical manifestations, divided into primary and secondary candidiasis. The main supply of C. albicans in the body is located in the gastrointestinal tract, and the development of infections occurs due to dysbiosis of the residential microbiota, immune dysfunction, and damage to the muco-intestinal barrier. The presence of C. albicans in the blood is associated with candidemia–invasive Candida infections. The commensal relationship exists as long as there is a balance between the host immune system and the virulence factors of C. albicans. This paper presents the virulence traits of Candida albicans and clinical manifestations of specific candidiasis. Keywords: Candida albicans, virulence traits, oral cavity, gastroenterology, dermatovenerology 1. Introduction 1.1. Fungal Infection Pathogens that causes fungal infections, such as Candida albicans, are widespread and may affect the skin and mucosal surface, and may cause systemic infection. Species of Candida are present in as many as 400,000 systemic fungal diseases [1]. Of all the species, Candida albicans is the most common causative agent of mucosal infections and systemic infection, and it is responsible for about 70% of fungal infections around the world [2]. It has been the leading cause of life-threatening invasive infections for the past several decades. Despite treatment, the mortality rate is close to 40%, especially in hospital conditions [3,4]. The present review aims to provide an overview of the virulence traits of Candida albicans and its clinical manifestations in the oral cavity, intestinal mucosa, skin, as well as in invasive infections. 1.2. Candida Albicans Candida albicans appears in several morphological forms (blastospores, pseudohyphae, and hyphae) (Figure 1). Blastospores divide asexually by budding [5,6]. During that process, new cell material is formed on the surface of the blastospore. The new bud grows from a small selected blastospore, and it is most often located distally from the site of a scar caused by birth, after which the phase of growth begins. After the growth phase ends, the cells divide, whereby the daughter separates from the parent cell by creating a partition [6]. Chains of elongated yeast cells characterize pseudohyphae, and the shape of hyphae is characterized by branched chains of tubular cells, with no narrowing at the sites of septation [7]. Filamentation is enhanced by a temperature higher than 37 °C, an alkali pH, serum, and high concentrations of CO2 [8]. In the same way, it is also enhanced by a lack of nitrogen and carbon in the presence of N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) [7]. This transition from a blastospore to a hypha is characterized by the activation of a complex regulatory network of signal paths, which include many transcription factors [8]. The main difference between yeast and hyphae composition is that the hypha wall has slightly more chitin content than yeast [9]. The cell wall is made of glucan, chitin, and protein. Its role is to protect the cell from stressful conditions in the environment, such as osmotic changes, dehydration, and temperature changes, and protect the cells from the host’s immune defense [10,11]. It is also responsible for adhesion to the host cell, with adhesion proteins such as Als1-7, Als9, and Hwp1 [12]. Communication of the cell with the outside environment takes place through the cell membrane [13]. Sterols in the cell membrane are extremely important, giving the cell stability, rigidity, and resistance to physical stressors [9]. Ergosterol is the most represented sterol and is characteristic for the cell membrane of fungi. It is synthesized on the endoplasmic reticulum and lipid bodies [14]. In the cell membrane, there is a phospholipid bilayer containing proteins with the role of receptors, but also some whose role is transport and also signal transduction [15]. In its metabolism, Candida albicans uses glucose as a source of carbon and amino acids as nitrogen sources [16]. 2. Virulence Factors of Candida albicans Candida participates actively in the pathophysiology of the occurrence and advance of infection, thanks to its virulence factors. One group of virulence factors causes colonization to take place, or the initiation of an infection, whilst the other group helps to spread the infection [17]. Polymorphism implies the transition of C. albicans from a commensal form to a pathological one, which depends on changes in the environment in which it is located. It is characterized by the morphological transition of blastospores into hyphae, and the transitional form between are pseudohyphae [18,19]. Asexual spores, chlamydospores, are formed under adverse conditions and are three to four times bigger than blastospores [12]. The morphological transition of C. albicans begins with the budding of blastospores and the formation of new cells. The nuclei separate at the mother–daughter cell junction via the septum [20]. fetched_contents.text: Native human and mouse skin infection models to study Candida auris-host interactions As the first-line defense barrier, the skin is facing life-long challenges by pathogens, including commensal microbial pathogens often forming an intrinsic part of the skin microbiome [1]. About a billion people worldwide are affected by superficial fungal infections, including skin as well as nails, and millions are affected by mucosal candidiasis [2]. Overall, several hundred million people are affected by fungal diseases and fungal-associated deaths exceed >1.5 million, which is similar to that of tuberculosis [[2], [3], [4], [5], [6]]. Elderly, preterm neonates and newborns, critically ill or immunocompromised patients are specifically vulnerable to fungal infections [5,[7], [8], [9], [10], [11]]. Of note, about 90 % of all reported fungal infections are caused by Cryptococcus species (spp), Candida spp, Aspergillus spp, and Pneumocystis spp [3]. Candida spp encompass more than 30 species with the potential to cause disseminated invasive infections of high morbidity and mortality in humans, with Candida albicans being one of the most prevalent human pathogens [3]. The US Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that approximately 25,000 cases of candidemia occur nationwide each year [2,12,13]. The mortality for candidemia disease ranges from an estimated 30–70 % depending on many factors, including hospital settings, type of patients, existing co-infections, early and fungal-specific diagnosis as well as proper antifungal therapies, just to mention a few critical factors that determine the outcome of fungal infections [14,15]. Of note, the epidemiology of Candida infections has changed in recent decades, with a shift from C. albicans to non-albicans Candida spp such as Candida glabrata [[16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21]]. C. albicans is a pleomorphic fungus obligatory diploid pathogen that can switch morphology between yeast, pseudohyphal and hyphal forms when encountering environmental cues or host-derived stimuli [22,23]. While yeast-like morphologies have been associated with commensal host colonization, hyphal morphologies are linked to pathogenicity [24]. Filamentous forms drive invasive diseases of high virulence owing to their increased tissue invasion capacities [25,26]. In addition, fungal morphologies strongly affect the degree of recognition and clearance by immune cells [22,24,27]. Candida auris is a newly emerging yeast-form pathogen showing pronounced adhesion to and almost predominant colonization of human skin [28]. A defective skin barrier enables C. auris to gain access to the blood stream, leading to disseminated diseases with mortalities ranging from 30 to 60 % [[29], [30], [31], [32]]. The marked skin adhesion traits explain the persistence and ease of transmission in healthcare settings. Most importantly, C. auris shows a remarkable propensity to acquire pan anti-fungal multidrug resistance phenotypes. While this often occurs in response to clinical antifungal therapy [28,33,34], a number of clinical isolates can display resistance to most antifungal drugs, including azoles, echinocandins flucytosine as well as amphotericin B [[35], [36], [37]]. Notably, the CDC [38,39] and the World Health Organization (WHO) [40] have ranked C. auris as “urgent threat” and “critical priority group”. Compared to C. albicans, C. auris is predominantly growing in the yeast morphology and seems incapacitated to form true hyphae [[41], [42], [43]]. However, C. auris can form pseudohyphal-like morphologies in response to high salt concentrations or genotoxins, suggesting that this morphological transition may occur under stressful conditions or when encountering host immune defense [43,44]. Still little is known about the ability of C. auris to penetrate epithelial or skin barriers in humans, although some human skin models, as well as some murine and porcine models exist [30,[45], [46], [47], [48], [49]], which enable studies of host defense mechanisms and fungal virulence. Some studies explored mechanisms of C. auris skin colonization by using synthetic sweat medium, mimicking axillary skin conditions [46]. In addition, transcriptional studies of a reconstructed three-dimensional human epidermis revealed changes to host gene expression in a C. auris colonized wound as well as up-regulated C. auris virulence genes [50]. Here, we developed novel skin models that enable comparative studies of C. auris adhesion and invasion of native mouse and human skin biopsies. Further, we implemented various established wound models that mimic nosocomial settings where skin barrier dysfunction or medical devices (catheters, post-operational-wounds, physical skin damage or burns) can facilitate or promote C. auris infections. Finally, these models offer a versatile toolset to study the action of drugs and compounds that can interfere or prevent C. auris colonization of human skin. 1. Materials and methods 1.1. Fetal back skin (15–17 weeks of estimated gestational age (EGA)), n = 3) was received after legal termination of pregnancy and processed as reported previously [51]. The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Medical University of Vienna (ECS 1969/2021; ECS 1760/2015) and conducted according to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki as well as written informed consent from participants and parents. Experiments with back skin from adult wild-type C57BL/BJ mice (age- and sex-matched, n = 3) were performed adhering to the ethical approval by the Medical University of Vienna and the Federal Ministry of Science and Research, Austria (BMBWF-66.009/0436-V/3b/2019). Experimental evidence supports studying Candida virulence factors independently of host immunity because virulence factors themselves are explicitly described as driving pathogenicity, while immune responses are framed as part of the broader host-pathogen balance. One direct line of evidence comes from reviews and primary literature that identify virulence traits as central to infection progression. The review on *Candida albicans* states that the commensal relationship exists as long as there is a balance between the host immune system and the virulence factors of *C. albicans*, and that these virulence factors lead to the development of candidiasis [N1-F1]. Another review emphasizes the interplay between Candida species and the host complement system, with complement evasion strategies as a major virulence mechanism [N4-R2]. A review on *Candida albicans* virulence factors also describes suppression and activation of host-acquired immunity, with secreted proteinases as a focal point for host interaction [N4-R3]. These sources together indicate that virulence factors are not merely passive markers but are central to infection, and that immune responses are part of the same host-pathogen interaction rather than an independent determinant of virulence.

The evidence also includes mechanistic studies showing that virulence factors drive pathogenesis. The *C. albicans* biofilm review notes that a major virulence attribute is the ability to form biofilms, densely packed communities of cells adhered to a surface [N2-R1]. Another article on biofilm formation describes the role of biofilm in pathogenicity and the challenges it poses [N2-R2]. A 2023 study on anti-biofilm and anti-hyphal efficacy shows that 3-hydroxy coumarin inhibits cell adhesion, morphogenesis, and hyphal formation in *C. albicans* [N2-R3]. A review on fungal biofilm formation summarizes the composition and function of EPS in biofilms and refines the formation process [N2-R4]. A review on targeting adhesion in *C. albicans* states that adherence and morphogenesis lead to biofilm formation and tissue invasion [N2-R5]. Taken together, these mechanistic studies show that specific virulence factors—adhesion proteins, morphogenesis regulators, hyphal formation, and biofilm-related traits—directly contribute to disease progression and that altering these traits can change infection phenotypes [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5].

Examples of altered virulence factors and changed infection phenotypes are strongest in biofilm and morphogenesis studies. The 3-hydroxy coumarin study directly demonstrates that reducing cell-adhesion and hyphal formation can suppress biofilm and hyphal growth [N2-R3]. The *C. albicans* biofilm review likewise frames biofilm formation as a core virulence attribute [N2-R1]. The *Candida albicans* virulence-factors review also notes that adhesion proteins such as Als1–7, Als9, and Hwp1 are involved in adhesion to the host cell, and that the cell wall protects the fungus from immune defense [N1-F1]. These examples support the idea that virulence-factor studies can be experimentally manipulated and phenotypically validated: changing adhesion, biofilm, hyphal, or morphogenesis-related traits changes the infection outcome [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R3].

The limitations of immune-competent host models are also evident in the evidence. Reviews repeatedly emphasize that virulence factors operate within a host-immune balance, which means immune responses can confound interpretation of virulence-factor effects [N1-R1][N4-R3][N4-R4]. The *C. albicans* virulence-factors review explicitly states that the commensal relationship depends on the balance between the host immune system and virulence factors [N1-F1]. Another review notes that Candida pathogenicity is induced and executed through interactions with host proteins and cells, and that the host responds in order to control infection [N4-R4]. A review on Candida biofilm formation and evasion of host immunity states that biofilms remain “hidden” from the host immune system and fail to activate host anti-Candida pathways [N3-R3]. These sources imply that immune-competent models may obscure the direct contribution of virulence factors because immune activation, clearance, and host response can alter the apparent infection phenotype [N1-F1][N4-R4][N3-R3]. In other words, immune responses may mask virulence-factor effects or even create alternative outcomes that are not attributable to the factor itself [N4-R3][N4-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports studying virulence factors independently of host immunity because virulence traits are central to disease, can be experimentally altered and phenotyped, and immune responses can confound interpretation. The strongest direct evidence comes from mechanistic studies of biofilm, adhesion, hyphal formation, and morphogenesis, while the limitations of immune-competent models are supported by reviews emphasizing host-immune balance and immune evasion [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5][N4-R3][N4-R4][N3-R3].

The review on Candida biofilm formation and evasion of host immunity adds that biofilms remain “hidden” from the host immune system and fail to activate host anti-Candida pathways [N3-R3]. This suggests that simplified models can reduce the influence of immune activation and clearance, preserving the direct contribution of virulence factors. The commentary on experimental mouse models of invasive candidiasis also states that such models are critical for understanding fungal pathogenesis and developing host defense strategies [N3-R5]. ### 5) Clinical and host-response evidence supporting prioritizing virulence factors over immune-response studies
Clinical and host-response evidence support prioritizing virulence factors over immune-response studies because specific virulence factors are linked to infection severity and host outcome, while immune responses can mask or alter the contribution of virulence factors. One direct clinical link is the study on *Candida* spp. isolated from candidemia, which evaluated exoenzyme production and biofilm formation capacity [N6-R3]. The 2025 study on virulence factors, biofilm formation, and antifungal resistance in *Candida* spp. reports that biofilm-forming capacity is significantly higher in *C. albicans* isolates from RVVC patients than in asymptomatic controls [N5-R2]. This indicates that virulence factors such as biofilm formation are associated with clinical disease severity and that their presence may predict worse outcomes [N5-R2]. The study on virulence factors of *Candida* spp. isolated from COVID-19 patients aimed to assess virulence factors and their associations [N5-R1], suggesting that virulence-factor profiles may be relevant to host outcomes in different clinical settings [N5-R1].

The evidence also shows that immune responses may mask or alter the contribution of virulence factors. The review on *C. albicans* virulence factors states that the commensal relationship exists as long as there is a balance between the host immune system and the virulence factors of *C. albicans* [N1-F1]. Another review on virulence factors and host immune response notes that the presented review describes the most important aspects of the still unknown pathogenicity of *Candida* associated with vaginal infections [N5-R3]. A review on *Candida* spp. and host immune response emphasizes the interaction between Candida species and the host immune system [N4-R2]. The review on Candida biofilm formation and evasion of host immunity states that biofilms remain “hidden” from the host immune system and fail to activate host anti-Candida pathways [N3-R3]. These sources together suggest that immune responses can obscure the direct role of virulence factors because immune activation, evasion, and clearance may alter the apparent infection phenotype [N1-F1][N3-R3][N4-R2]. In other words, immune responses may not simply reflect the infection; they may also change how virulence factors are expressed or detected [N1-F1][N3-R3].

### 6) Why virulence-factor studies are still necessary even when immune responses are present
Virulence-factor studies are still necessary even when immune responses are present because virulence factors are central to the pathogenic process. The *C. albicans* virulence-factors review states that virulence factors are part of the transition from commensal to pathogenic behavior and that they lead to the development of candidiasis [N1-F1]. The biofilm review frames biofilm formation as a major virulence attribute [N2-R1]. The anti-biofilm study shows that altering adhesion and hyphal formation changes biofilm and hyphal phenotypes [N2-R3]. The review on complement evasion and host immunity emphasizes complement evasion strategies as a major virulence mechanism [N4-R2]. These studies show that virulence factors are not merely downstream consequences of immune activation; they are drivers of disease and can be manipulated experimentally [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-R2]. Even in immune-competent settings, understanding virulence factors is necessary because they explain the mechanisms of infection, tissue invasion, and immune evasion, and they may provide targets for intervention that immune-response studies alone cannot capture [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-R3].

### Bottom line
The evidence supports studying Candida virulence factors independently of host immune responses because:
- virulence factors directly drive disease and can be experimentally altered to change infection phenotypes [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5];
- immune responses can confound interpretation by obscuring the direct contribution of virulence factors [N1-R1][N4-R3][N4-R4][N3-R3];
- host-independent models such as human/mouse skin biopsies and wound models reduce confounding while preserving pathogenesis-related behaviors [N3-F2][N3-R2];
- comparative studies show species- or strain-specific virulence traits, biofilm formation, and clinical outcomes [N5-R4][N6-R3][N5-R2];
- clinical evidence links virulence factors to infection severity and host outcome, while immune responses may mask or alter their contribution [N5-R2][N5-R1][N1-F1][N3-R3].

In short, virulence-factor studies are foundational to understanding Candida infection because they reveal the mechanisms by which the fungus causes disease, even when immune responses are present [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-R2].
